verses.translation_literal: After these things the word of YHWH was to Abram in the vision, saying: Do not fear, Abram; I [am] a shield for you; your reward [is] exceedingly great.
verses.translation_dramatic: After all of this had passed, after the battle smoke had thinned and the kings were gone, a word came to Abram. It came not as a voice from a mountain but as a vision: the LORD himself, speaking. "Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your shield. And what I hold for you is very great indeed."
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the first time Genesis uses the formula "the word of YHWH came" and the first time it says a word came "in a vision" (machazeh). Previously God simply spoke to Abram; now the prophetic category appears, and Abram is being treated as a prophet. Play it as an intimate, vulnerable moment, not as thunder.

"After these things" ties the scene to the war with the four kings in chapter 14. Rashi, Rashbam and Radak all hear a man afraid: afraid of revenge from the kings' relatives, or afraid that he had spent his merit on the victory. Ramban adds a second fear, dying without a child. A man who refused the king of Sodom's goods (14:23) has just given up a payout; "your reward" answers that. In the ancient Near East a shield (magen) is what a soldier holds up between himself and death, so God offers himself as the equipment of a man who has just gone to war.

The KJV makes the last clause "thy exceeding great reward", turning God into the reward. The Hebrew has a verb form, harbeh, here pointed as an infinitive ("making great"), so most modern renderings read it as a clause "your reward will be very great". The KJV's version is possible, but it hides how ambiguous the Hebrew is. Note "fear not" is also the standard opening of salvation oracles: it tells the actors this is a comfort speech.

philological_notes.note: A prophetic vision, from the verb 'to see'. It occurs only a few times in the Bible and is a rarer word than 'mar'eh'. Radak stresses that this is the first vision in which Abram is shown things, not only told them (the walk outside, the stars, the animals).
A small shield. As a metaphor for God it recurs in the Psalms (for example 'YHWH is my shield'). Here it is a promise of protection after a battle.

verses.translation_literal: And Abram said, My Lord YHWH, what will you give to me, and I am going childless, and the son of Meshek of my house, he [is] Dammeseq Eliezer.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Abram answered, and there was an ache beneath the courtesy. "My Lord, LORD — what can you give me? Look at me. I go on my way childless. The one who will stand at the door of my house when I am gone, who runs it now, who comes and goes in it — he is Eliezer. Eliezer of Damascus."
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this as grief spoken politely, not as rebellion. Abram has just heard that his reward will be very great (v.1), and he answers with the one thing wealth cannot buy. In the ancient Near East a man without a son did not simply lose his name: his land, flocks and the care of his burial went to someone else. Adoption of a household member as heir was a known remedy, and Abram is looking at it with dread rather than hope. Radak hears the question as being about this world, not the next: what good is all this riches if strangers eat his labor tomorrow?

The Hebrew of the last clause is knotted, and the KJV smooths it. Word for word it runs "and the son of meshek of my house, he Dammeseq Eliezer". The KJV turns it into a tidy "steward of my house" and joins the clauses with "seeing", which makes Abram's complaint a logical argument; the Hebrew only says "and", and lets the grief pile up in short phrases. The sound is the clue: meshek (with shin) and Dammeseq (with sin) chime, and the line seems to be made of that echo. Rashi follows the Targum: the household is fed by his word, and he is a man from Damascus (Rashi notes the Targum reading and that Abram pursued the kings as far as Damascus); the Talmud reads the name as an acronym, "he draws and gives to drink" from his master's teaching to others. Radak gives two ways to take "Dammeseq Eliezer": a Damascene (with the ending dropped, as Onkelos translates), or a man whose first name was Dammeseq and whom Abram renamed Eliezer, a Hebrew name. Either way the point is the same: the heir is a foreigner. "Lord God" in the KJV hides two different words: adonai, the title, and the divine name written beside it. Radak notes that for God the title comes before the name, unlike other beings, for whom the name comes first.

philological_notes.note: 'Childless'; the word is rare and its root is disputed. Menachem ben Saruq takes it as a heir-less state, Rashi's own view connects it with stripping and desolation (cf. 'ar'ar, to be bared). Ibn Ezra treats the final yod as a suffix of the same kind as in 'akhzari'. The KJV's 'childless' gives the sense and loses the bareness.

An obscure phrase, glossed 'the one who runs back and forth' in my house. Radak derives meshek from the root shaqaq, one who comes and goes; Ibn Ezra derives it from the same root; Rashi follows the Targum: the whole house is fed at his word. The sound answers Dammeseq in the same line.

Two names side by side. Radak: either 'a Damascene' with the ending dropped, or a man first called Dammeseq whom Abram renamed. Rashi: the Targum takes it as from Damascus, and the Talmud reads an acronym. The identity of this Eliezer with the servant of Genesis 24 is not stated in this verse.

token_glosses.gloss: Meshek (the one who runs / acquisition) of

verses.translation_literal: And Abram said: Look, to me you have not given offspring, and look, the son of my house is inheriting me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Abram said it again, lower this time, and with nothing left to hide. "Look. You have given me no child. And look who stands to inherit everything I am."
verses.directors_commentary:
He says it a second time, with the same opening word ("and Abram said"), and strips the complaint down. There is a pause between the two lines; the actor should not rush it. "Hen" and "hinneh" are both "look", and Abram uses them like pointing fingers: first at his own empty hands, then at the servant in his tent.

The KJV gives "one born in my house is mine heir." That harmonizes with the later laws of household slaves, but the Hebrew says only "the son of my house", which could be a slave born in the household or one bought in. And "is mine heir" is a present participle: "is inheriting me". It is already happening. Radak is careful to say Abram is not accusing God of lying; he is wondering whether he has forfeited the promise.

philological_notes.note: 'To inherit, to take possession.' The same root recurs in verses 4, 7 and 8 and carries the chapter: who inherits Abram, and who inherits the land.

verses.translation_literal: And look, the word of YHWH [was] to him, saying: This one will not inherit you; but [one] who will come out from your inward parts, he will inherit you.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then, before the silence could settle, the word of the LORD came to him again. "This man will not be your heir. Only one who comes from your own body will inherit you. He will."
verses.directors_commentary:
The answer arrives on top of the complaint. Ramban notes the "and look" here: Abram's words are still in the air. There is no argument, no rebuke. The voice is simply specific: not the servant, not an adopted son, but a child of your own body.

The KJV's "out of thine own bowels" is, for once, close to the Hebrew. The word me'im means the inner organs, and the Hebrew uses it of the place from which a child comes. Radak notes it points to the reproductive organs; Ibn Ezra calls it a metaphor for the organ nearby. Modern versions that say "your own son" lose the physical edge. The repetition of "he will inherit you" at the start and end frames the verse like a seal.

philological_notes.note: From 'me'eh', the inner organs, here standing for the loins or womb. Isaiah 48:19 uses the related phrase 'those who come out of your inward parts' of descendants (Radak cites it).

verses.translation_literal: And he brought him out to the outside and said: Look, please, toward the heavens, and count the stars, if you are able to count them. And he said to him: Thus will your offspring be.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then he led Abram out of the tent, into the open night. "Look up," he said. "Look at the sky and count the stars, if you can." Abram looked, and could not. "So," said the voice, "will your children be."
verses.directors_commentary:
The staging matters. God moves Abram from the closed tent, where he has been counting what he lacks, into the open, where he can see more than he can count. The "na" ("please") is gentle, almost coaxing, which is rare in a divine command. "If you are able" is a challenge and an invitation. Abram cannot count; that is the whole point.

The KJV's "tell the stars" uses an old sense of "tell" = count, so a modern audience hears something else. "Thus" (koh) is a gesture, as if a hand is waving at the sky. Radak notes this vision happens inside the prophetic vision, and later in the chapter it is still day (verse 12 says the sun is about to set); Radak reads the whole as one vision, and Rashi gives a midrash that God lifted him above the stars. Mesopotamian astrology (Abram is a man from Ur of the Chaldeans) read fate in the stars, so here the Creator of the stars is naming a fate.

philological_notes.note: 'Look attentively'; the Hiphil of 'nabat' means to look attentively, and the 'na' softens the command into a request.
'Count'. The same root yields 'sefer' (book) and 'mispar' (number); the verb is a counting, not a telling. The KJV 'tell' is an obsolete sense.

verses.translation_literal: And he believed in YHWH, and he reckoned it to him [as] righteousness.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Abram believed. He had nothing in his hands but a word, and he believed the LORD. And it was counted to him, set down to his account, as righteousness.
verses.directors_commentary:
One of the shortest and most weighty verses in the book, and it should be played quietly. Abram has been standing under the stars; there is no sign yet, no son, no change. He trusts. Radak says the trust was complete this time, after the earlier doubt, because the LORD now said "from your own body" and showed him the stars.

Who reckons what is not settled by the Hebrew. The second verb has no named subject. Rashi, Radak and Sforno read it as God: He counted Abram's trust as merit and righteousness. Ramban disputes Rashi, whom he quotes and does not follow, and prefers Abram as the one who reckons: Abram believed the LORD and reckoned that God would give him a seed out of God's own righteousness, not because of Abram's deserving; Ramban also offers the other reading, that God counted the promise as righteousness. The KJV's "counted it to him for righteousness" inserts "for", which is not in the Hebrew (the verb takes "it", "to him" and "righteousness" directly), and it settles the matter in God's favour, as a bookkeeping entry. Note also "believed in": the verb comes from the root of "amen" and means to take as firm, to lean the weight on something; it is closer to trust than to assent. For an ancient audience, who weighed righteousness as faithfulness inside a relationship, this is a covenant word.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of the root of 'amen': to treat as firm and trustworthy, to rely on. Followed by 'in YHWH' (be-). The plain vav with a perfect, not the narrative form, sets the verse apart from the story line; this reading is my own.

'And he reckoned it'. The subject is unnamed. Rashi, Radak and Sforno: God counted Abram's trust as righteousness and merit. Ramban rejects Rashi's explanation and prefers: Abram believed, and he reckoned that God's own righteousness would give him a seed; or God counted His promise as righteousness, as with Phinehas (Psalm 106:31).
Righteousness, right standing, what is owed in a relationship. Ibn Ezra compares Deuteronomy 6:25, 'and it shall be righteousness for us'.

verses.translation_literal: And he said to him: I [am] YHWH who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land to take possession of it.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the voice said, "I am the LORD. I am the one who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, so that I might give you this land, and that you might possess it."
verses.directors_commentary:
The second promise opens like a royal charter: "I am YHWH who brought you out". This is the pattern of an ancient suzerainty treaty, where the great king introduces himself and recalls what he has done before he states what he asks. The same formula opens the Ten Commandments ("I am YHWH your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt"). The echo is intentional: the God of the exodus is already, in Abram, the God of an earlier exodus.

The KJV's "to inherit it" is right in sense, but note that the same Hebrew root yarash, used for the heir in verses 3-4, now means to take a land. The question of who inherits Abram turns into the question of who inherits Canaan. "Ur of the Chaldeans" was a major city of southern Mesopotamia. Genesis 11 says Terah took the family from there; here God says that he did it. Ibn Ezra notes that it is Ur, not Haran, that is named.

philological_notes.note: Infinitive with a suffix: 'to take possession of it'. It echoes the inheriting of verses 3-4 and sets up the question of verse 8.

verses.translation_literal: And he said: O Lord YHWH, by what will I know that I will take possession of it?
verses.translation_dramatic: And Abram said, "Lord, LORD, how will I know? How can I be sure that it will be mine?"
verses.directors_commentary:
Abram has just been credited with faith, and now he asks for proof. Do not play it as a lapse. Radak and Sforno both insist he does not doubt; he asks about the how. The formal address returns ("Adonai YHWH", as in verse 2), the sign of a man asking a serious question to a king.

The KJV's "whereby shall I know" is archaic: it means "by what means". The Hebrew is literally "in what will I know", and the answer in verse 9 is a ritual, not a sign. In the ancient world a land grant was confirmed with a formal act, and Abram is asking for the legal form. Ramban reads it as asking for the guarantee of a covenant that cannot be broken by later sin. Contrast Gideon, who asked for a sign in Judges 6 and was given one.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'in what?', that is, 'by what means?'.

token_glosses.gloss: I will take possession of it

verses.translation_literal: And he said to him: Take for me a heifer threefold, and a she-goat threefold, and a ram threefold, and a turtle-dove and a young bird.
verses.translation_dramatic: The answer was not a word but a task. "Bring me a heifer, a she-goat and a ram, each of them three, and a turtle-dove, and a young pigeon."
verses.directors_commentary:
God does not argue. He gives an order, and the order sets the scene for a covenant ceremony. "Take for me": the animals are for God, so Abram is being asked to prepare an offering. The list names the animals that the later law of Leviticus allows for sacrifice: cattle, goats, sheep, and the two birds that the poor may bring.

The KJV, ASV, Webster and BBE all say "three years old". The Hebrew word meshullash means "made threefold" or "third", and it is not the usual way of saying someone's age. Onkelos and Radak read "three of each" (three heifers, three goats, three rams), and Ramban notes that a three-year-old cow would not be called an eglah (young heifer) at all. The Hebrew allows both, and a director should know the line is disputed. The birds are "a turtle-dove and a young bird" (gozal). Rashi and Onkelos take the gozal to be a young pigeon; Radak notes the word can be any fledgling, but pigeons are what the law accepts.

philological_notes.note: From 'three'. It can mean 'threefold' / 'of three', or 'three years old', and the packet's authorities split: Onkelos and Radak say three animals each, Ibn Ezra and others say three years old.
A fledgling; the same word is used for the eaglets in Deuteronomy 32:11. In the offering laws the bird is a young pigeon.

verses.translation_literal: And he took for him all these, and cut them in pieces in the middle, and set each piece of it to meet its fellow; and the bird he did not cut in pieces.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he took them all — every one that had been named — and, one by one, he cut them through the middle. He laid each half facing its fellow, so that a lane lay open between the rows. But the birds he left whole.
verses.directors_commentary:
The actors should not hurry this. No one explains why Abram does what he does: the LORD said only "take" in v.9, and Abram, who needs no further instruction, cuts. Radak says everything he cut and everything he spared was at God's command, though the text does not say so. This is a covenant scene. In the world of Abram's day, one cut the animals and walked between the halves to bind an oath, calling down the animals' fate on oneself if the oath were broken; Jeremiah 34:18 shows the same rite, and Rashi draws the line to it. The phrase "to cut a covenant" comes from this very act, and the KJV's "divided them in the midst" hides how raw the Hebrew verb is: batar, to cut apart, rare outside this chapter and Jeremiah.

The detail that matters is the birds. The Hebrew says "the bird", a collective, and the KJV's plural "birds" is fair; but it says nothing of why. The law of the burnt offering is the plain reason: Ramban notes that of the offered fowl it is said "he shall not divide it" (Leviticus 1:17), so the birds are laid out whole. Rashi and Radak read it as a sign. Rashi: the nations are bulls, rams and goats, and Israel is the dove (Song of Songs 2:14), so the beasts are cut up and the bird is not: the nations will be destroyed, Israel will endure. Radak: the nations are divided and set against one another, and will wear themselves out; Israel is one people, one law, wherever it is scattered.

philological_notes.note: 'And he cut in pieces', the intensive stem; the object pieces are called bitarim. Ibn Ezra compares 'the mountains of Bether' (Song of Songs 2:17) and 'between its pieces' (Jeremiah 34:18).

Literally 'a man, his piece, to meet his fellow': each half is set opposite its pair. Ibn Ezra explains 'ish' as 'the one belonging to', as in 'a man of war'. The idiom 'each... its fellow' is used also of things, not only people.

A general word for a bird, here singular and collective. Ibn Ezra: it means the turtledove and the young pigeon of v.9. Ramban: the birds are not cut because of the rule 'he shall not divide it' (Leviticus 1:17).

verses.translation_literal: And the bird of prey came down on the carcasses, and Abram drove them away.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the birds of prey came down on the dead. And Abram drove them off.
verses.directors_commentary:
A small, physical beat, and a good one for the actor: hours pass, the meat lies in the heat, and the scavengers arrive. Abram is a man waving his arms against birds. It is a moment of guarding, of watching, with nothing happening but waiting for God.

The KJV's "the fowls" is archaic for birds in general, but the Hebrew ayit is specifically a bird of prey, a raptor, and it is singular and collective: "the bird of prey". It is the word Jeremiah 12:9 uses of the hostile birds. "Carcasses" (pegarim) usually means whole dead bodies, a point that Radak makes to say the birds attacked the whole birds; Rashi says the halves. The verb vayyashev, "he blew away" or "drove off", is rare and carries the sense of blowing a breath. The KJV's "drove them away" is fair. Later Jewish readers heard a hint of enemies of the offspring being beaten back, as in the Targum.

philological_notes.note: A bird of prey. Rashi connects it to the verb 'to swoop' (as in 1 Samuel 15:19). The singular is collective.
Corpses or carcasses, normally whole bodies. Radak takes it to mean the whole birds, Rashi the halves; the word is not decisive.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, the sun [was] about to go in, and a deep sleep fell on Abram, and look, dread, great darkness, falling on him.
verses.translation_dramatic: The sun was going down. A deep sleep fell upon Abram, and with it came a dread, a great darkness, pressing down upon him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns. After a long day of waiting, the sun sinks and the stillness becomes frightening. The sleep is not rest. The word tardemah is the sleep God sent on Adam (Genesis 2:21) and a sleep that belongs to God's work; it is a trance in which something is done to a man. What falls on him is not sleep alone but terror.

The KJV's "an horror of great darkness" is memorable, but the Hebrew has three nouns in a row without any "of": emah, chashekhah, gedolah, "dread, darkness, great". The grammar piles them up, as if the fear came in layers. The verb "falling" is repeated: sleep fell, and the dread is falling, in a participle that makes it continuing. Ramban and Rashi hear in the darkness a hint of later exile; Radak reads the shift from good news to hard news. Whichever reading you use, the actor has gone from hope to a shaking dread, and the director should hold it before verse 13 speaks.

philological_notes.note: A deep, God-sent sleep, as in Genesis 2:21 and 1 Samuel 26:12; in prophetic scenes (Daniel 8:18) it comes with the vision.
A string of three nouns. Radak reads it as 'dread and darkness, great'; the midrash in Ramban assigns each word to a kingdom of the later exiles. The grammar itself has no 'of'.

verses.translation_literal: And he said to Abram, Knowing, you shall know that a sojourner will your seed be in a land not theirs, and they will serve them and they will afflict them, four hundred year.
verses.translation_dramatic: And out of that darkness a voice spoke to Abram. "Know it. Know it fully. Your children will be strangers in a land that is not theirs. They will be made to serve, and they will be pressed down hard — four hundred years."
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the voice from the dark, and the actor must not soften it: the promise of the land comes wrapped in a long grief. After the sleep and the dread of v.12 the LORD speaks, and He begins with an emphatic: yado'a teda', "knowing, you shall know", the Hebrew doubling of the verb that makes a thing certain. The KJV's "Know of a surety" is an archaism for it, but it keeps the force.

Two words deserve attention. A ger is not a tourist: he is a resident alien, with no land of his own and no clan to protect him. And "afflict" translates 'inu from 'anah, to press down and humble. Hearing it is meant to connect forward to Egypt. Who does the serving? The suffix on va'avadum is open. Radak gives both readings: the verb can mean that the Egyptians will make use of Israel's labour ("they shall be enslaved among them", as Onkelos has it, the sense of working through someone), or, without the missing preposition, that Israel will serve the Egyptians, who then afflict them with hard labour; the KJV's "shall serve them" keeps the same openness and does not decide.

The number is the old puzzle. Rashi counts four hundred years exactly from the birth of Isaac, Radak likewise, and counts 210 in Egypt itself. Ramban says the verse is transposed: "a sojourner... in a land not theirs for four hundred years", and the serving and affliction follow without a stated length. He also reports Ibn Ezra's view, four hundred years from this day. Land that is "not theirs" is not named as Egypt: Rashi points out that Isaac and Jacob were also sojourners in Canaan. Sforno adds the reason for the delay: the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet complete.

philological_notes.note: Infinitive absolute with the finite verb: an emphatic 'you shall surely know'. The solemnity marks that what follows is a settled decree, not a threat.

A sojourner: a resident alien without land or tribe. Ibn Ezra relates it to a seed cut from its branch (a 'grain'), the opposite of 'ezrach', one rooted like a tree. Rashi notes that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were each called 'ger' in the land.

'And they will serve them', with an object suffix that does not say who serves whom. Radak: either the verb stands for 'work through them' (the Egyptians exploit Israel; Onkelos 'they shall be enslaved among them'), or it has no missing preposition and means Israel serve the Egyptians, who afflict them with hard labour.
'And they will afflict', from 'anah, to press down and humble. The same verb as Sarai's treatment of Hagar in Genesis 16:6 and a keyword of the Exodus story.

verses.translation_literal: And also the nation which they will serve, judging [am] I; and after thus they will go out with great property.
verses.translation_dramatic: "But that nation, the one they serve, I will judge. I myself. And when it is done, they will walk out, and they will not walk out empty-handed. They will carry great wealth with them."
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse turns on a single word, 'also' (וְגַם). The oppressor is not excused because the exile was foretold. Ramban reads it as: though I decree this, I will still judge the nation that carries it out, because they will do more than was ordered. The pronoun is stressed too: 'judging, I' (דָּן אָנֹכִי), the participle placed before the subject, so that the actor must put the weight on God Himself as the judge, not on some court of the nation's own.

KJV 'will I judge' is accurate, but it renders a participle as a future and drops the sense of something already in motion. 'Substance' (רכוש) in KJV is a seventeenth-century word for property; the Hebrew is moveable goods, the livestock, silver and gold of a household, which is exactly what a refugee would carry. Rashi connects the 'great property' with the despoiling of Egypt in Exodus 12.

In a world where slaves left with nothing, and where a freed slave was sent away with at most a small gift, this is an extraordinary promise: they leave as a people with their wealth, not as runaways.

philological_notes.note: A participle 'judging' with the pronoun after it: God Himself is the judge. Ramban reads this as the judgement of the nation that exceeds its decree.
Moveable property: livestock, goods, silver. Rashi links it with the Egyptians being stripped of their goods at the Exodus.

verses.translation_literal: And you, you will go to your fathers in peace; you will be buried in good grey hair.
verses.translation_dramatic: "And you, Abram, you will not see it. You will go to your fathers in peace. You will be laid in the earth in a good old age, with white hair and a full life behind you."
verses.directors_commentary:
After the long shadow of the last two verses, one personal sentence. The pronoun is stressed (וְאַתָּה, 'and you, you'), a deliberate contrast with 'your offspring': the hardship will fall on them, and on him there will be peace. The line should be delivered close and warm.

'Go to your fathers' is a euphemism for dying, and KJV keeps it. But it is easy to hear it as a plain statement of travel. Radak and Ibn Ezra take it as an idiom for death, as in 'gathered to his people'; Rashi, the midrash, hears in it a hint that Abram's father Terah repented. That is a tradition, not the plain sense. 'Buried' matters too: the Hebrew thinks of a proper burial in the family tomb as the mark of a good death, which is why it is a blessing, and why the later purchase of Machpelah matters.

KJV's 'a good old age' loses the Hebrew image: שֵׂיבָה is literally the grey or white hair of old age, the crown of a long life. Abram was 'at peace' in the sense of שלום, wholeness and without violence.

philological_notes.note: An idiom for dying. Radak compares 'gathered to his people' and God's words to Josiah.
Literally 'in good grey hair', that is, a good old age; Radak glosses it as living to see children and grandchildren.

verses.translation_literal: And [the] fourth generation, they will return here, for not [is] complete the iniquity of the Amorite until here.
verses.translation_dramatic: Not you, Abram, and not your sons at once. The fourth generation will turn and come back to this ground. The wait has a reason: the guilt of the Amorite is not yet full. It has not yet reached its measure. Until that hour, not yet.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the promise comes with a delay, and the delay is given a reason. For Abram, a long wait would sound like abandonment; the LORD answers that he is not late, the Amorites' wrongdoing is simply not yet full. The picture is of a measure filling toward its brim, and it is justice on a timetable: in the ancient world a people was not expelled for no reason, and a god who waited before judging was showing both patience and fairness. The KJV's 'in the fourth generation they shall come hither again' is close, but 'again' is not in the Hebrew; the verb is simply 'they will return' (yashuvu), and the 'hither' is the land where Abram stands. 'Not yet full' also adds 'yet'. The Hebrew says 'is not complete until here', a verb of completeness (shalem, the root of shalom) applied to guilt, a dark twin of the word for peace in verse 15.

What is the fourth generation? Rashi counts it from the descent into Egypt, through Judah, Perez, Hezron and Caleb, so that Caleb son of Hezron is among those who enter the land. Ibn Ezra reads 'generation' as a span of dwelling and counts Kohath, Amram, and Moses with Aaron. Rashbam and Ramban both take the four generations to be the Amorites', not Israel's: a period of grace in which the nations might yet turn back, on the principle of visiting iniquity to the third and fourth generation. The Hebrew alone does not say whose four, and a hearing audience would sense both. Notice, too, that 'Amorite' stands for all the peoples of Canaan, as is common in Genesis; Ibn Ezra and Radak both say the strongest of the nations is named for the whole.

philological_notes.note: A 'generation', but also a span of dwelling or an age. The verse gives no figure in years beyond the 'four hundred' of verse 13. Commentators disagree on whether it counts a hundred years (Rashbam), a lifetime of dwelling (Ibn Ezra) or the descent from Judah to Caleb (Rashi).

'Complete' (shalem) is the root of 'peace' and 'payment'; here it is applied to 'iniquity', which can mean the wrong itself or the punishment it earns. Radak reads 'iniquity' as the penalty, as in 'my iniquity is greater than I can bear' (Gen 4:13). The picture of a measure being filled is Rashi's, who cites Isaiah 27:8.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, the sun had gone in, and thick darkness was, and behold! a smoking fire-pot and a torch of fire which passed between these pieces.
verses.translation_dramatic: The sun had gone down. Night closed over the hill, thick and black, with no star to break it. And then, out of the darkness, a smoking fire-pot, and a flaming torch, moving slowly between the severed halves of the animals.
verses.directors_commentary:
The staging is everything here. The pieces are the halves of the animals Abram laid out earlier in the chapter; in an ancient covenant ceremony, the parties walked between the cut halves, calling down on themselves the fate of the animals if they broke their oath. Ibn Ezra says plainly that this was the oath; Jeremiah 34:18 describes the same rite with a calf.

What is startling is who walks: not Abram, who is asleep, but the fire and smoke, the sign of God. Ramban reads this as the Presence itself passing between the pieces. The one making the oath is God, alone, and Abram is the witness. KJV 'smoking furnace' and 'burning lamp' are decent but lose the setting: the Hebrew תַּנּוּר is a fire-pot or oven that gives off smoke, and לַפִּיד is a torch, the thing carried at night.

The word 'darkness' (עֲלָטָה) is a rare, heavy word for pitch dark; Radak calls it the strongest darkness. KJV flattens it to 'it was dark'. The accent on 'had gone' (בָּאָה) marks a completed action, as Rashi and Radak observe: the sun had already set. Give the lights time to appear.

philological_notes.note: Thick darkness, a rare word. Radak: the strongest darkness, with not even starlight.
A smoking fire-pot or oven; Ibn Ezra imagines a figure like an oven giving off smoke with a torch inside. Ramban compares Ezekiel 1:4 and Sinai.
Between the pieces: the halves of the sacrificed animals, the setting of a covenant oath. Ibn Ezra equates the pieces with the oath; Radak says the parties passed between the halves.

verses.translation_literal: On that day YHWH cut with Abram a covenant, saying, To your offspring I have given this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates:
verses.translation_dramatic: On that very day the LORD cut a covenant with Abram, and spoke it aloud: "To your children I have given this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates."
verses.directors_commentary:
The idiom is 'cut a covenant' (כָּרַת בְּרִית), and every English reader should hear it. KJV has 'made', which hides that the verb is the one for cutting, and for the severed animals of the verse before: a covenant is cut because blood is shed to make it. This is the verse where the earlier image is named.

The tense matters too. God says 'I have given' (נָתַתִּי), a perfect, not 'I will give' as in earlier promises (12:7, 13:15). Ramban makes this point, and the shift fits a covenant oath: the gift is spoken of as done, though the possession is far off. Rashi says that a divine word is as if already done.

The boundaries: the 'river of Egypt' is probably a wadi on the southern edge of Canaan, not the Nile; Ibn Ezra argues for שיחור, a different name, though that identification is his. The Euphrates is called 'the great river', and Rashi and Radak explain that it is 'great' because it touches the land of Israel, quoting the saying that 'a king's servant is a king'. This describes the most extravagant bounds of the land in the Bible, as a promise and not as a map.

philological_notes.note: 'Cut a covenant': the verb is the one for cutting, tied to the severed animals of verse 17. KJV 'made' loses this.
Perfect: 'I have given'. Ramban notes the contrast with the future 'I will give' of earlier promises; Rashi: the Most High's word is as if done.
'River of Egypt'. Ibn Ezra takes it as שיחור and not the Nile (היאור).

verses.translation_literal: [obj] the Kenite and [obj] the Kenizzite and [obj] the Kadmonite,
verses.translation_dramatic: The Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites,
verses.directors_commentary:
The speech now becomes a list, and a list read aloud is a drumbeat: the promise is made concrete by naming the people who live on the land. Do not rush it. Each name is a family with a camp and a tent, and each is part of the promise.

The first three are the odd ones. Neither the Kenizzites nor the Kadmonites ('easterners') appear in the usual lists of seven peoples; ten are named here, and Rashi, quoting the midrash, says the extra three were to be given later. The Kenites were nomads, in later texts friendly to Israel (Radak notes their intermarriage with Judah and the house of Rechab, 1 Chr 2:55). KJV's plural 'Kenites' is a convenience; the Hebrew has the singular, as a collective.

philological_notes.note: The Kenite, named from Cain/Kain (קַיִן), which Radak links to a city. Later friendly to Israel.

verses.translation_literal: And [obj] the Hittite and [obj] the Perizzite and [obj] the Rephaim.
verses.translation_dramatic: The Hittite, the Perizzite, and the Rephaim, the tall ones, the old ones of the land. The list ends on a name that sounds like giants.
verses.directors_commentary: The list of ten peoples closes here with the Hittites, the Perizzites and the Rephaim. A boundary-and-peoples list like this one was how land was conveyed in a treaty: naming those who live there made the grant exact. 'The Hittite' here is of Heth, son of Canaan (Gen 10:15), a Canaanite group in the hills; whether this is the great Anatolian empire is not settled by the verse. The Perizzites are linked with the open country and villages. The KJV prints 'the Rephaims', but Rephaim is already a plural in Hebrew, so the 's' doubles it. The word is often translated 'giants', as in the Targums (Onkelos: gibbaraei), and elsewhere in the Bible it can also mean the shades of the dead, a double sense an ancient hearer would feel. Rashi links them to the land of Og (Deuteronomy 3). Radak notices that the Hivites are missing from this list and wonders whether they are meant by the Rephaim. Ibn Ezra reads the ten as the same peoples counted in different ways elsewhere: seven in some lists, ten here.

philological_notes.note: A plural people-name, 'the Rephaim'; the KJV 'Rephaims' doubles the plural. The Targums render it 'giants'. Rashi ties it to the land of Og, called the land of the Rephaim in Deut 3.

verses.translation_literal: And [obj] the Amorite and [obj] the Canaanite and [obj] the Girgashite and [obj] the Jebusite.
verses.translation_dramatic: The Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites, the Jebusites. Ten peoples, named one by one, and every name a promise.
verses.directors_commentary:
The list ends on the Jebusites, the people of the city that would one day be Jerusalem. The Amorite returns here, the same people whose guilt was 'not yet full' in verse 16; the listener hears the two verses answer each other.

Note 'Canaanite', which is both one people in the list and the name of the whole land. Ibn Ezra explains that after the six smaller names the Canaanite stands for those who remain; Radak adds that the Philistine territory counts within it (Joshua 13:3). Ten names in all (verses 19-21) is a full number: the entire land, nothing held back. KJV's English plurals ('Amorites') turn a collective singular into a head count; the actor can let the singular stand and hear a whole people in one word.

philological_notes.note: The Canaanite: one people among ten, and the name of the whole land. Ibn Ezra: after six named peoples, 'Canaanite' covers the rest; Radak: Philistine land is counted within it.

events.title: The LORD tells Abram in a vision not to fear
events.narrative_summary: After these things the word of the LORD comes to Abram in a vision. The LORD tells him not to fear, for he is Abram's shield and his reward will be very great.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Cue: 'After these things' (15:1), with no interval and no hour. Anchored on the END of Abram's refusal of the spoils (Gen 14:21-24) with an offset of 1 year and a margin of 3 years, so the window (about 2 to 4 years after Gen 14) reaches toward Gen 16:3 (Abram 85, ten years in Canaan); the vision may fall anywhere in that span. The night time_of_day (ASHMORET_HATICHONAH, 22:00) is set because the stars of 15:5, in the same exchange, need night; it is a reading, not a datum. MACRO_ERA, because the text gives only a sequence word.

events.title: Abram protests that he is childless and Eliezer his heir
events.narrative_summary: Abram asks what the LORD will give him, since he goes childless and the heir of his house is Eliezer of Damascus. He repeats that he has been given no offspring.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the vision at once: the same dialogue, no time word (15:2-3). Anchored on the END of the vision with no offset. DAY_SEQUENCE, because the scene belongs to the day of 'that day' (15:18).

events.title: The LORD promises Abram a son and as many offspring as the stars
events.narrative_summary: The word of the LORD answers that Eliezer will not inherit, but a son from Abram's own body. He brings Abram outside to count the stars, promises that his offspring will be so many, and Abram believes, and it is credited to him as righteousness.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Answer in the same exchange (15:4-6), no time word. Anchored on the END of the complaint. The stars of 15:5 need night, so this scene falls in the night that begins with the vision (22:00); the duration of 8 hours runs it to about dawn, because the following scenes (15:7ff) take place in daylight on the next day, ending with the sunset of 15:12. The event is thus the night of the vision, not eight hours of speech. The 'that day' of 15:18 is then the day of the sunset covenant.

events.title: The LORD promises the land and Abram asks how he will know
events.narrative_summary: The LORD says he brought Abram out of Ur of the Chaldeans to give him this land to possess. Abram asks how he will know that he will possess it.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Continuous speech, no time word (15:7-8). Anchored on the END of the previous exchange, no offset. Ten minutes for two short speeches.

events.title: Abram prepares and halves the animals and drives off the birds of prey
events.narrative_summary: The LORD tells Abram to bring a three-year-old heifer, goat and ram, a turtledove and a young pigeon. Abram brings them, cuts the animals in two and lays the halves opposite each other, but not the birds. Birds of prey come down on the carcasses and Abram drives them away.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Command and execution are continuous (15:9-11), with no gap. Anchored on the END of Abram's question, no offset. The duration of 3 hours is an estimate (the text gives none) of the fetching, the cutting and the watching. It must end before sunset (15:12), and the dry run shows it ending c. 17:08, before the 18:00 sunset.

events.title: A deep sleep and great dread fall on Abram at sunset
events.narrative_summary: As the sun is about to set a deep sleep falls on Abram, and a horror of great darkness falls on him.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Cue: 'when the sun was going down' (15:12). Anchored on the END of the animals event with time_of_day EREV (18:00), so it starts at the first sunset at or after the end. Duration 3 hours covers the sleep in which 15:13-18 happen. Margin 30 minutes, since the text pins the hour only roughly.
events.ancient_diurnal_marker: When the sun was going down

events.title: The LORD foretells exile, deliverance, Abram's peaceful death and the fourth generation
events.narrative_summary: The LORD tells Abram that his offspring will be sojourners in a land not theirs, enslaved and afflicted four hundred years. He will judge the nation they serve, and they will leave with great possessions. Abram will die in peace in a good old age, and in the fourth generation they will return, when the Amorites' iniquity is full.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Spoken during the deep sleep (15:12-13). A child of the sleep event, anchored on its START with an offset of 15 minutes, so inside the parent. No hour of its own, so DAY_SEQUENCE.

events.title: A smoking furnace and a flaming torch pass between the pieces
events.narrative_summary: When the sun has gone down and it is dark, a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch pass between the animal pieces.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Cue: 'when the sun had gone down and there was thick darkness' (15:17). A child of the sleep event, anchored on its START with an offset of 1 hour (the sun has set, full darkness), margin 30 minutes. DIURNAL_HOUR, because the text names the hour of the night.
events.ancient_diurnal_marker: When the sun had gone down and it was dark

events.title: The LORD makes a covenant giving Abram's offspring the land
events.narrative_summary: On that day the LORD makes a covenant with Abram: to his offspring he gives this land from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates, the land of ten peoples that the text names.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Cue: 'On that day' (15:18). The covenant words follow the passing of the fire and so come at the end of the same night. Anchored on the END of the passing, no offset. DAY_SEQUENCE.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: Abram's refusal of the spoils (14:23) and the risk it brings are answered by the LORD's promise to be his shield and reward (15:1).
Abram's complaint that his servant will inherit is answered by the promise of a son from his own body (15:4).
The halved animals laid in two rows (15:10) make the path between the pieces that the fire passes through (15:17).
Abram's question 'whereby shall I know?' (15:8) is answered by the command to bring the animals (15:9).
The fire passing between the pieces is the covenant rite, and the LORD then states its terms (15:17-18).
The promise of a great reward moves Abram to ask what it can be, as he is childless (15:2).

entities.summary_bio: A torch of fire that passes between the divided animal pieces together with the smoking furnace. It is the second sign in the darkness before the covenant.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew tannur is a portable oven or fire pot; ashan means smoke.
entities.summary_bio: A smoking fire pot that appears in the darkness after sunset and passes between the divided pieces. It appears with the flaming torch just before the LORD's covenant.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew ayit means a bird of prey.
entities.summary_bio: Birds of prey that come down on the carcasses Abram has laid out. Abram drives them away.

entities.etymology_meaning: Not a name; the group of a heifer, a she-goat, a ram, a turtledove and a young pigeon.
entities.summary_bio: The animals the LORD tells Abram to bring: a heifer, a goat and a ram, each three years old, plus a turtledove and a young pigeon. Abram halves the three animals and sets the pieces opposite each other; the birds are left whole.
The Girgashites are one of the Canaanite peoples listed as holding the land the LORD promises to Abram's offspring. They are named only in the lists of peoples.

entities.etymology_meaning: From Yebus, the old name of Jerusalem; its meaning is uncertain.
entities.summary_bio: The Jebusites are the last of the ten peoples listed in the covenant's land grant. They are named here only in the list.
The Kadmonites are one of the ten peoples listed in the land boundaries of the covenant. They are named only here in the Bible.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably related to qayin, 'smith'; this is uncertain.
entities.summary_bio: The Kenites are the first of ten peoples listed as living in the land promised to Abram's offspring. Here they appear only in that list; elsewhere they are a people later linked with Moses' father-in-law (Judg 1:16).

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably from the name Kenaz, an Edomite clan name.
entities.summary_bio: The Kenizzites are listed among the peoples whose land the LORD gives to Abram's offspring. They appear only in this list.

The offspring of Abram are the descendants promised to him: a son from his own body, then as many as the stars. The LORD says they will be sojourners in a land not theirs for four hundred years and then receive the land.
The unnamed nation that will enslave and afflict Abram's offspring in a foreign land. The LORD says he will judge it, after which the offspring leave with great possessions.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew Kasdim, the name of the Chaldeans; its origin is uncertain.
entities.summary_bio: Chaldea is the southern Mesopotamian region named in the phrase 'Ur of the Chaldeans'. It appears here only as the origin from which Abram was brought out.

entities.etymology_meaning: Meaning uncertain; the name may relate to a Sumerian city name.
entities.summary_bio: Ur is the city in Mesopotamia from which the LORD says he brought Abram out. The LORD cites it as the ground of his right to promise the land.

Eliezer is the member of Abram's household whom Abram names as his heir while he has no child. The text calls him 'Damascus Eliezer' and 'the son of the acquisition of my house'. The LORD answers that he will not be the heir.

components.label_value: Eliezer, a servant born in his house
components.evidence_explanation: Abram names the household servant Eliezer as his heir (15:2-3), and the LORD rejects him at 15:4.

components.label_value: A son from his own body
components.evidence_explanation: The LORD says 'he that shall come out of your own body shall be your heir' (15:4).

components.label_value: In covenant with the LORD over the land
components.evidence_explanation: 'On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram' giving his offspring the land (15:18).
Abram says 'I go childless' and 'to me you have given no seed' (15:2-3).
'He believed in the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness' (15:6).
Abram 'cut them in the middle' and set each piece opposite the other (15:10).

systems.name: Covenant cutting
systems.ancient_near_east_context: In Hebrew a covenant is 'cut' (karat berit). Near Eastern treaties were sealed by dividing animals and walking between the pieces, a self-curse for breaking the oath (compare Jer 34:18-19).
rules_and_mechanics: Animals are divided in two and the halves set opposite each other.
The parties pass between the pieces to bind themselves by oath.
Carcasses are guarded until the rite is complete.

systems.name: Faith reckoned as righteousness
systems.ancient_near_east_context: The verb 'to reckon' (chashav) is accounting language, and in priestly texts a offering or act is 'reckoned' as acceptable (Lev 7:18). Here trust in the LORD's promise is counted as righteousness.
rules_and_mechanics: The person trusts the LORD's word about something not yet seen.
The LORD credits that trust as righteousness.
No act or ritual is required for the reckoning.

systems.name: Revelation in a vision or deep sleep
systems.ancient_near_east_context: In the ancient Near East, divine messages often came in dreams, visions or deep sleep. Genesis marks them with the words 'vision' (machazeh) and 'deep sleep' (tardemah), as at Gen 2:21 and Job 4:13.
rules_and_mechanics: The word of the LORD comes to the person and speaks to him.
The recipient may answer and question the speaker.
A state of sleep or dread may accompany the message.
The message can reach beyond the present to the future of descendants.

systems.name: Request for a sign
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Asking God for a confirming sign is a recurring pattern (Gideon in Judg 6, Hezekiah in 2 Kgs 20). The request is for assurance, and the answer is often a ritual or a wonder.
rules_and_mechanics: A person asks how he will know a promise holds.
The request is addressed to the LORD directly.
The LORD may answer with a ritual action rather than an explanation.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Abram brings the five animals, halves three and sets the pieces opposite each other, and drives away birds of prey.
system_instances.significance_note: It prepares the covenant-cutting rite the LORD completes at 15:17.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Abram believes the LORD and it is counted to him as righteousness.
system_instances.significance_note: A key verse of Genesis: righteousness rests on trust in the promise.

system_instances.outcome_summary: A smoking furnace and a flaming torch pass between the animal pieces in the dark.
system_instances.significance_note: It ratifies the covenant by a sign of the divine presence; Abram does not pass.

system_instances.outcome_summary: In deep sleep Abram hears that his offspring will be sojourners and servants four hundred years, then leave with great possessions in the fourth generation, and that he will die in peace.
system_instances.significance_note: It gives the Exodus a place in the plan and explains why the land is not yet given (the Amorites' iniquity is not full).

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD says Eliezer will not inherit, a son from Abram's own body will, and shows him the stars as the measure of his offspring.
system_instances.significance_note: It answers Abram's complaint and gives the offspring promise its concrete image.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD makes a covenant with Abram and gives his offspring the land from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates, listing ten peoples.
system_instances.significance_note: It turns the promise of the land into a covenant with fixed boundaries.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Abram asks how he will know that he will possess the land.
system_instances.significance_note: It prompts the covenant ritual that follows.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The word of the LORD comes to Abram in a vision and tells him not to fear, because the LORD is his shield and very great reward.
system_instances.significance_note: It opens the chapter and the first direct address of the LORD to Abram after the war of Genesis 14.

edges.description: Abram asks by what he will know that he will possess the land.
Abram drives the birds of prey off the carcasses.
Abram asks what the LORD will give him while he is childless and his heir is a servant.
The LORD tells Abram to bring a heifer, goat, ram, turtledove and young pigeon.
The LORD makes a covenant with Abram, giving the land to his offspring.
The LORD reckons Abram's belief to him as righteousness.
The LORD tells Abram that his offspring will be sojourners and servants in a foreign land for four hundred years.
The LORD promises Abram a son from his own body and offspring like the stars.
The LORD, who brought Abram out of Ur, says he will give him this land to possess.
The LORD tells Abram not to fear, because he is his shield and great reward.
